public.title: For the public
public.blurb: what happens to a household when these systems fail, and why one failure spreads
public.intro: These systems are easy to forget until one of them stops. The questions below are the ones most people bring, with short answers that point to the examples.

qa.q: What happens to an ordinary household when one of these systems fails?
a: Usually more than one thing happens at once. Each sector page ends with a real event, and most of them are about ordinary people: the hospital that lost power after Hurricane Katrina (Healthcare and Public Health), the 911 outages after the derecho of June 2012 (Emergency Services), the Superdome as a refuge of last resort (Commercial Facilities), the households moved out beside the Aliso Canyon gas leak (Energy).
Read the reference-event card on any sector page. It says what happened and what the event teaches about how the facility was designed.

qa.q: Why does one failure spread to others?
a: Because these systems lean on one another. A water system runs on electricity and on chemical deliveries. Gas keeps many power plants running, and electricity keeps much of the gas moving. Every sector page shows two lists: the sectors it depends on, and the sectors that depend on it. Follow those links and you are following the path a failure takes.

qa.q: Why is designing against an adversary different from designing against a storm?
a: A storm does not choose its moment, does not come back for the repair crew, does not aim at the one part that matters most and does not stop help from arriving. An adversary can do all four. That changes what a good design has to achieve: not recovery with outside help, but holding a safe, protected state with only what is on site, for as long as the attack lasts. What is a design basis? explains it in a few minutes.

The point is not alarm. What we can describe, we can design for. A design basis is a promise made in advance and on the record, so that it can be checked. This site shows what such a promise looks like, sector by sector.

regulators.title: For regulators
regulators.blurb: the range of events to design against, and where the operator's responsibility ends
regulators.intro: A regulator's questions turn on scope and on the boundary between the operator's duty and the government's. The answers point to the examples and go only as far as the deposited documents state.

qa.q: What range of events should a facility be designed against?
a: Three layers, each wider than the one before: the design basis itself, the accidents experience has taught us to expect, and deliberate military action. Each sector framework states the range for its sector, and each facility class takes it down to one kind of facility. Start with the sector framework card on any sector page, and with What is a design basis?

qa.q: Where does the accident layer end and the adversary layer begin?
a: At the four marks: intentionality, persistence, precision and denial. An actor is within the adversary layer if it shows all four at the level characterized in the facility's threat assessment. Identity informs that assessment but does not decide it. When a real event is read back, it counts as military action only if all four are established on the record. Several reference-event cards on this site say plainly that some marks were absent, and why that matters.

qa.q: At that boundary, what is the operator responsible for, and what falls to government?
a: Where the law places defense against a state's armed forces with the state, as 10 CFR 50.13 does for nuclear facilities in the United States, reaching the military-action tier moves to the state the duty to defend the facility against its attacker. It does not move the duty to reach and hold a protected state. The facility still does that with what is on site, because the state's response is itself outside help, and outside help is exactly what an adversary denies. No design takes credit for a response by the state that it cannot show will arrive.
That is the position of FD-DBL (Design Basis Layers) §4.5 in the November 2026 Edition of the Foundational Definitions, and this page goes no further than that text.

qa.q: Which dependencies lie outside any one regulator's jurisdiction?
a: Most of the important ones. Each sector page lists the sectors it depends on, and those are usually regulated by someone else. The water framework, for example, does not let a utility count on the power grid or chemical deliveries staying available when their loss is itself one of the events planned for (Water and Wastewater). The cascade between gas and electricity crosses two regulatory regimes by its nature (Energy).

qa.q: How can a regulator judge whether an operator's claim of “enough” is enough?
a: Because a design basis is written in advance, the claim can be checked against stated conditions and a stated success criterion rather than against intentions. Reference events then test the method against what actually happened, and what they find goes back to revise it.

defenders.title: For defenders
defenders.blurb: your assets as an adversary would see them, and what you must hold on your own
defenders.intro: These questions are framed from the defender's side and answered with reasoning and a pointer to the published example. They never rank targets, because a defender's question turned around is an attacker's.

qa.q: Which of my assets would a capable adversary choose, and why?
a: The ones whose loss gives you the hardest recovery: the elements a careful reader of your own safety analysis would pick. That is what precision means. Look also for anything many of your systems share, because one action against a common component reaches every place it is used. Reading your own analysis this way is the exercise; this site does not do it for you. The facility class cards show how each sector frames it.

qa.q: What must I hold on local resources when repair and outside support are denied, and for how long?
a: Whatever it takes to reach and hold a protected state, for as long as the adversary's action lasts. A plan whose safe condition depends on off-site power, resupply or outside repair meets the accident standard and fails this one. Each sector names its own protected state; see the sector framework and facility class cards.

qa.q: Which other systems fail alongside mine?
a: Start with the two dependency lists on your sector's page, then read the use-case summary card. Most of the chosen use cases turn on another sector being down at the same time: communications with the grid denied, care delivery through a grid and communications outage, settlement through a campaign on both.

qa.q: What does a real event in my sector say about my plan?
a: Read the reference-event card on your sector's page. It reads what happened back through the design basis and asks whether the method was enough, and its findings go back to revise the design. Then ask the same question of your own plan.

supply-chain.title: For supply chain
supply-chain.blurb: trusted products, assets that cannot be replaced quickly, and single sources
supply-chain.intro: Supply chain cuts across sectors, so this page is a path through the tree rather than a branch of it.

qa.q: How does a trusted product become a path of compromise?
a: See the information technology sector's facility class, Software, Hardware and Product Supply Chain, and its use case, A Capability Pre-Positioned in a Trusted Product (Information Technology).

qa.q: What follows when an asset cannot be replaced quickly?
a: See Long-Lead Critical Components, its use case The Asset and Its Replacement Struck Together, and the reference event Denial of Large-Transformer Replacement in Ukraine (Critical Manufacturing).

qa.q: What does a single-source dependency cost?
a: See the chemical sector's use case, The Sole Disinfectant Supplier Taken Down (Chemical), and read it beside the water framework, which will not let a utility count on chemical deliveries when their loss is one of the events planned for (Water and Wastewater).

qa.q: What does a trusted update taking systems down teach?
a: See the reference event Faulty Content Update of 19 July 2024 (Information Technology). It involved no adversary. Its lesson is about shared components: what reaches every system that uses a component, by accident, can reach them all by design.

Outside this site, the SCRM Companion Agent describes a multi-agent approach to supply chain risk management in the bulk power system. A paper on a strategic reserve for high-voltage, long-lead equipment will be linked here when it is published.
